script_segment: The year is 1824 and you are born in Southwark, London,
on the wrong side of the river.
Your home smells of tar, wet wool,
and the Thames at low tide. Your father is a cooper.
He bends oak staves into barrels for the breweries along the bank.
He is a broad, silent man who believes any problem can be
solved with a hammer and enough patience. Your mother takes in washing.
Her hands are always red, always cracked, and always moving.
She has one saying, and she says it every single day.
Keep moving, love. Standing still is for the dead.
You take her seriously. Maybe too seriously.
By age 4, you can outrun the dog.
By age 7, you can outrun the boys twice your age.
You race them across London Bridge, dodging carts, horses,
and old women with baskets of eels. You lose a shoe once.
You win anyway. By age 10,
the local shopkeepers pay you a penny
to run messages across the river,
because you get there before the ink dries.
Your father watches you sprint down the lane one evening and
says the only compliment you will ever hear from him.
That boy's legs are worth more than my whole workshop.
He's right.
In a city like London, a poor boy only owns two things.
His back and his legs. And yours are excellent.
Years pass and you turn 16.
You become a porter at Billingsgate Market.
Every morning before dawn, you carry baskets of fish on your head,
stacked three high,
through crowds so thick you could walk on their shoulders.
It's brutal work, but you're fast. The fastest.
The fishmongers fight over you.
You earn enough to give your mother half your wages.
She stops taking in so much washing. Her hands begin to heal.
For the first time in your family's history, things are getting better.
Then comes the autumn of 1846.
It's a Tuesday.
You're cutting through the docks to save time, as you always do.
Above you, a crane swings a crate
of Portuguese wine off a ship. You hear a rope snap.
Someone shouts. You look up.
Big mistake.
The crate lands on your right leg just below the knee.
You don't feel it at first. You just hear it.
A wet crack, like a barrel stave splitting in the cold.
Then you look down and see something
white sticking out of your shin.
It takes you a moment to understand it's your bone.
Then you feel it.
The dockworkers lift the crate off you.
One of them takes one look at
your leg and turns away to vomit.
Another ties his neckerchief around your thigh.
They put you on a cart and someone says
the word you have heard all your life,
the word every poor Londoner fears more than prison. Hospital.
In 1846, hospitals are not for people like you.
Not unless someone important says so.
To be admitted as a charity patient,
you need a letter from a subscriber,
a wealthy donor who pays for the right to recommend the poor.
Without that letter, the hospital owes you nothing.
Your father runs. You've never seen him run before.
He goes to the brewery owner he's made barrels for
these past twenty years and stands in the man's doorway,
hat in hand, until he gets the letter. It takes four hours.
You spend those hours on the kitchen table at home,
biting a wooden spoon while your mother holds
your hand and tells you to keep breathing.
She doesn't say keep moving.
For the first time, she doesn't say it.
By nightfall, you're admitted to University College Hospital.
The first week is disorienting in the best possible way.
You have a bed. An entire bed, to yourself.
The sheets are clean, mostly.
A nurse brings you beef tea every morning
and a pint of porter beer every evening. A pint of beer.
In a hospital. Doctors prescribe it to keep your strength up.
You decide that whoever invented hospitals was a genius.
A young house surgeon examines your leg.
He presses on the swelling and says it's a compound fracture,
which means the bone broke through the skin.
He says some surgeons would take the leg off immediately,
but he'd like to try to save it. He sets the bone.
You scream so loudly the whole ward goes silent.
Then he splints it, bandages it, and pats your shoulder.
You'll keep it, he says. Probably.
You hold onto that word for days. Probably.
The man in the bed next to you is called Silas.
He's old, at least sixty,
with white whiskers and a face like a walnut.
He is missing his left leg from the knee down.
He lost it at Trafalgar in 1805, he tells you,
to a French cannonball that came through the
gun deck while he was loading powder.
He's back now because the stump has
opened up again after forty years,
and the surgeons want to trim it.
Trim it, he says, like it's a hedge.
Silas has opinions about everything.
He says the beef tea is boiled boot leather.
He says the house surgeon is too
young to grow a proper beard,
and a man who can't grow a
beard shouldn't be trusted with a saw.
He says the porter beer is the
only honest thing in the building.
Then he asks if you're going to finish yours.
You laugh.
You hadn't realized how long it had been since you laughed.
He tells you stories at night when the ward is dark.
About sailing past Gibraltar.
About eating ship's biscuits so full of weevils that the crew would
tap them on the table and race the bugs that crawled out.
About Admiral Nelson, who got seasick every single voyage of
his career and still won every battle. Silas says that's the lesson.
You can be sick, scared, and miserable, and still win.
You believe him.
Then, in your second week, you hear the bell.
It rings from the top of the building,
a sharp bright clang that cuts through the whole ward.
The nurses stop what they're doing.
The men in the beds stop talking.
Someone near the window crosses himself.
Silas doesn't look up from his beer. Operating day, he says.
A few minutes later, you hear it.
Faintly, through two floors of brick, a man screaming.
It goes on for what feels like forever. Then it stops.
Not fades, but stops. Silas finally takes a sip.
You ask him if the man died. He says, probably not.
Usually it just means they're finished.
You lie awake that night staring at the ceiling,
listening to your own heartbeat. You're not thinking about the man upstairs.
You're thinking about your leg.
Because the smell has started.
It's faint at first.
Sweet and rotten, like fruit left in the sun.
The nurse changes your dressings and doesn't say anything,
but you notice she breathes through her mouth.
The swelling spreads up past your knee.
The skin around the wound turns from red to purple to
a shade of grey that doesn't belong on anything alive.
Your fever arrives on the twelfth day and doesn't leave.
The house surgeon comes back. He doesn't press on anything this time.
He just looks. Then he says he'll speak to Mr. Liston.
Silas goes very still.
Robert Liston, he tells you, is the most famous surgeon in London.
Possibly the world.
Six foot two, hands like shovels, and the fastest knife in Britain.
Silas has heard he once took off
a leg in under thirty seconds.
He says students come from all over
Europe just to watch him work.
He says it like it's good news.
You ask him why it doesn't sound like good news.
Silas thinks for a long time.
Then he tells you about the operating theatre.
In 1846, there is no way to
put a person to sleep for surgery.
No gas, no injection, no anything. You are awake. Completely awake.
The only mercy a surgeon can offer is speed.
The faster he cuts, the less you feel,
the less blood you lose, and the less likely you are to
die of shock on the table.
So when Silas says Liston is fast,
what he means is that Liston is the best thing that
can happen to you in the worst room in London.
He gives you advice. Drink all the brandy they offer.
Bite down on the leather and don't let go of it,
because men have bitten through their own tongues.
Don't look at the saw.
Look at a spot on the ceiling and count.
And whatever happens, don't fight the dressers,
the students who hold you down.
They're stronger than you, and fighting only makes it last longer.
You nod. You've never been told anything that sounded more
like a death sentence in your life.
That Thursday, the bell rings for Silas.
He's in good spirits.
He tells the nurse she looks lovely, which she doesn't,
and tells you to save him a beer, which you will.
Two dressers help him onto a stretcher.
At the doorway, he turns around and gives you a salute,
the proper naval kind, sharp and crisp.
Keep moving, sailor, he says. You never told him your mother's saying.
He just said it.
You hear him upstairs. Not for long. He's an old sailor.
He's done this before.
They bring him back an hour later, grey and sweating, but alive.
He opens one eye and asks for his beer.
You hand it over, and you both laugh, and for one evening,
everything is fine.
Then the fever comes for him too.
It isn't his stump. It's the hospital.
In 1846, nobody knows what germs are.
Surgeons wear the same frock coat for every operation,
stiff and black with years of old blood,
and they consider this a badge of honour.
The more blood on the coat, the more experienced the surgeon.
Nobody washes their hands.
The same sponges are used on wound after wound.
Doctors call what happens next hospital fever,
and they accept it the way they accept the weather.
Silas burns for six days.
On the fifth night, he talks to people who aren't there.
He gives orders to men who drowned forty years ago.
On the sixth morning,
his bed is empty and the sheets have been changed,
and nobody says anything about it.
His beer sits untouched on the shelf above
his bed until a nurse takes it away.
You don't cry. You've stopped crying.
The fever in your leg has climbed to your thigh,
and you're too tired for grief.
You just stare at the empty bed
and think about what he said.
You can be sick, scared, and miserable, and still win.
You decide to believe him. You don't have a choice.
The next Monday, Mr. Liston himself comes to see you.
He's even bigger than Silas described. He fills the doorway.
He has a calm, almost bored expression,
like a man looking at a broken fence.
He peels back the dressing, sniffs once, and covers it again.
He tells you plainly that the leg
must come off above the knee, and that if it doesn't,
the rot will reach your blood and
you'll be dead within the week.
Then he tells you the surgery will be on Wednesday,
in front of the students.
He says it like he's offering you a seat at the theatre.
Which, technically, he is.
Your parents visit that night. Your mother holds your hand.
Your father stares at your leg and
says nothing for a long time.
Then he leans in and tells you
he'll make you a new one. Oak. The best oak in Southwark.
He says it'll be the finest leg in London.
You laugh. He doesn't. He means it.
Your mother kisses your forehead and whispers, keep moving, love.
On Wednesday morning, the bell rings.
The nurse gives you a glass of brandy, then another.
You drink both. The house surgeon gives you a dose of laudanum,
which makes the ceiling soft at the edges,
but does nothing for the dread.
Two dressers lift you onto a stretcher
and carry you up the stairs. You count them. Forty-two steps.
The operating theatre is round, like a small arena.
Wooden benches rise in steep tiers all the way to the skylight,
and every one of them is full.
Medical students, maybe two hundred of them, packed shoulder to shoulder.
Some are eating. Some are taking notes.
At the back, someone shouts heads, heads,
and the front rows duck so the back rows can see.
In the middle of it all is the table.
Plain wood, stained dark. Beneath it, a wooden box filled with sawdust.
You know what the sawdust is for.
They strap you down.
Leather across your chest, your arms, your good leg.
Four dressers take position, one at each limb.
One of them slips a strip of leather between your teeth.
He's young, barely older than you, and his hands are shaking.
Then Mr. Liston walks in. The room goes silent.
He takes off his jacket and puts on his operating coat,
and it's exactly as Silas described.
Stiff, black, and crusted with the blood
of a thousand people before you. The students lean forward.
Liston selects a long,
thin knife from his case and holds it between his
teeth while he ties the tourniquet around your thigh.
Then he turns to the benches and says, Time me, gentlemen.
The students pull out their pocket watches.
You look at the ceiling.
You find a spot, a small brown stain near the skylight,
and you start counting.
One.
The knife goes in.
There is no word in English or any
other language for what that feels like.
It's not pain the way a stubbed toe is pain.
It's the whole universe pouring into one place.
Your back arches so hard the straps creak.
You bite down on the leather and taste blood.
The dressers lean on you with their full weight.
Two. Three. Four.
You can hear it. That's the part nobody warns you about.
You can hear the knife moving through you.
A soft, wet sound, like your mother wringing out washing.
Seven. Eight.
Liston calls for the saw. Somebody hands it to him.
You stop counting.
The sound of the saw on your bone
is the loudest sound you have ever heard. Louder than the docks.
Louder than the crane. Louder than the bell.
It goes on and on and on,
and then there's a thud in the sawdust beneath the table,
and you understand the thing that thudded used to be you.
Then the needle. The stitches. The bandages.
And then a student calls out, from
somewhere high above you, the number. Twenty-eight seconds.
The room applauds.
They are applauding.
You lie on the table, soaked in sweat and brandy and blood,
while two hundred young men clap for the
man who just sawed off your leg.
Liston gives a small nod, wipes his knife on his coat,
and walks out without looking at you.
That's how they all remember him. The fastest knife in London.
They carry you back down the forty-two stairs.
You don't count them this time.
The first few days are almost hopeful. The stump is clean.
The fever drops.
The house surgeon says you're healing beautifully and the nurse
brings you two pints of porter instead of one.
You start thinking about the oak leg your father promised.
You picture yourself back at Billingsgate. Not running, not anymore, but walking.
Working. Moving.
Your mother visits and laughs for the first time in a month.
Then, on the ninth day, you feel the chill.
That deep, shaking cold, even with three blankets on.
You know what it is.
You've watched it happen once already, in the bed beside you.
The fever comes for you the way it came for Silas.
Quietly at first, then all at once.
The stump turns hot and swollen and starts to smell sweet.
The nurse starts breathing through her mouth again.
The doctors try everything they know.
They bleed you, which makes you weaker.
They give you more brandy, more laudanum, more beef tea.
They're not cruel.
They're just doing exactly what doctors have done for three hundred years,
and none of it was ever going to work.
On the night of December 20th, 1846,
you dream that you're seven years old,
racing across London Bridge with both your legs. You're winning.
You can hear your mother laughing somewhere behind you,
telling you to keep moving.
You don't wake up.
And here's the part nobody tells you.
The very next morning, on December 21st, 1846, in that exact
same operating theatre, up those exact same forty-two stairs,
Mr. Liston takes off the leg of a butler named Frederick Churchill.
But this time, the patient doesn't scream.
Two months earlier, a dentist in Boston demonstrated something new.
A gas called ether.
You breathe it through a glass jar, and you fall asleep,
and you don't wake up until it's over.
The news took weeks to cross the Atlantic by ship.
It arrived in London only days ago.
Frederick Churchill breathes the ether,
falls asleep on the same table you were strapped to,
and feels absolutely nothing. When he wakes up,
he asks when the operation is going to start. The students laugh.
Liston turns to them and says that
this Yankee trick beats mesmerism hollow.
The room applauds again.
You missed it by one day.
If the crate had fallen a few weeks later,
if the fever had arrived a little slower,
if a ship had crossed the Atlantic a little faster,
you would have slept through the whole thing.
Within a year, ether is used in hospitals across Britain.
Within twenty years,
a surgeon named Joseph Lister convinces surgeons to finally clean their hands,
their instruments, and their wounds. Within a century,
nobody in London is ever strapped awake to that table again.
Historians will write about December 21st, 1846,
as one of the greatest days in medical history.
They'll print Frederick Churchill's name in textbooks.
They'll call Robert Liston a legend.
They'll print his time on your leg as a fun fact.
Twenty-eight seconds.
Nobody will write down your name.
But in a barrel workshop in Southwark,
an old cooper finishes carving the finest oak leg in London.
He sands it smooth for weeks.
He never once lets it out of his sight.
And he never tells anyone who it was for.
